chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from his brother Al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Zakat becomes permissible for the owner of seven hundred [dirhams] and prohibited for the owner of fifty [dirhams]. I said to him, 'How can this be?' He said: 'If the owner of seven hundred has many dependents, and if he were to distribute it among them, it would not suffice him, so he should spare himself [from giving it away] and take it for his dependents. As for the owner of fifty, it is prohibited upon him if he is alone and is a craftsman/tradesman, working with it, and he attains from it what suffices him, God willing.'
ai.seo_question: Can a person with wealth still receive Zakat?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the Shia jurisprudential principle that Zakat eligibility is determined by net sufficiency rather than gross wealth, emphasizing the role of dependents and earning capacity. It highlights the scholarly distinction between a wealthy individual with high maintenance burdens who may receive Zakat, and a self-sufficient artisan with minimal assets who is prohibited from taking it. This reflects the practical application of the Quranic verse 9:60, ensuring aid reaches those in genuine need despite their nominal asset levels.
